Or more likely, you could generate an image that's sort of like the daydreaming that a child engages in—and that daydreaming, that's a waking dream. It'll be in images, like a moving picture. Well, moving picture, a movie is actually a collective dream. That's another way of thinking about it. And so the birthplace of your hypothesis about what your better future could be will make itself manifest in the form of a vision. Literally.
4.85: And people have visions all the time. It isn't how we describe them. When you're reading a book, a novel, the characters come to life in your imagination. That's a vision. When you daydream, that's a vision. It's a form of thought. But it's also a form of revelation, partly because—why revelation? Well, it has an autonomy, and you know this. If you fantasize, if you fantasize sexually, there'll be a part of that that's voluntary. You set up the image, let's say, but it'll play itself out as if it has its own autonomy, its own characterization.
4.86: People who write novels report this all the time. They don't know what the hell is going to happen to the characters. The story unfolds in their imagination. They capture it in words. There'san in-built dynamism that's autonomous in the fantasy. And one of the reasons that people have a religious impulse, you might say, is because they've noted over millennia that that process of fantastic approach to the solution of problems has an autonomy.
4.87: So what would you say? It's characterized by a spirit that's not exactly you, in the same way that your conscience isn't exactly you, or in the same way that things that grip your interest aren't exactly you. Jung, when he talked about the collective unconscious, his hypothesis was that the deeper reaches of the collective unconscious constituted the spirit that makes itself manifest in everyone, that generates the fantasies that constitute the initial solutions to the problems of life. So it's tied deep down into the instinctual substrate, and there is an autonomy to that.
4.88: And Jung's proposition was that the entity that people regard as God is the concretization of that autonomy of spiritual development. Brilliant, a brilliant hypothesis. I also think that one that's irrefutable. OK, so back to this statement. Ask and it shall be given to you. OK, so what does this mean? It means that you actually have to ask. You might say, well, this has never worked for me. It's like, well, first of all, that's not true because you think, and now and then that works. And you might ask yourself, well, how well could you think if you were really thinking?
4.89: And really thinking might be, "I'm asking a dead serious question here, and I'm willing to accept any answer whatsoever, as long as I find it credible and motivating, no matter what I have to give up." And that's a sacrificial gesture. And maybe you're very unhappy in your marriage and you're trying to figure out why and you think, "Oh my God, I'm at the end of my bloody rope. I'll do anything to fix this."
4.90: And then you have a fantasy, and God only knows what that is. And if you don't do that, maybe it'll be a murderous fantasy because that's when the problem-solving mechanism has been suppressed enough and lied about enough to start to become seriously pathological. You might want to consult yourself with a little bit more regularity before it comes to that. But the fantasy will make itself manifest and there'll be things that you have to change. And those are parts of you that you— parts of you that you have to let die. And that's part of the pain of thought, and it's part of the pain of genuine conversation with people.
4.91: Because maybe you're sitting down with your wife trying to sort through what the hell went wrong, and you find out that there's parts of you, buddy, they really have to go. And those might be like limbs, not just like fragments of your being, whole parts of you that have to burn away. God, it's no wonder people don't want to do that. But, so, how do you put yourself in a position where you're willing to ask? I would say, well, one of the things you can do is you could use some terror on your side. So here's something to contemplate. You can try this.
4.92: It's kind of interesting. You might have to practice it a bit before you get good at it. So, imagine you sat down and you allowed yourself to think about all the stupid things you do that you know are stupid. There's going to be things you do you don't know. And maybe it's because you're blind or you're ignorant or whatever, but there's some things you're doing for sure that you know are stupid.
4.93: And there are also some of those things that you could stop doing, but for whatever reason, don't. And then you might think, OK, imagine I let those things have free rein. I just stop resisting them. I let them take me wherever the hell they're actually aiming. What would that look like five years down the road? Now, everyone's temperament predisposes them to a different domain of temptation. So for example, if you look at narcissistic people, so narcissistic people want unearned attention and they want unearned status, OK?
4.94: And then you might say, well, what are the personality predictors of narcissism? And if you're extroverted and disagreeable, you're more likely to be narcissistic. And then you might think about that as a form of genetic determinism, because whether you're extroverted is like 50% genetic, and whether you're disagreeable is 50% genetic. And that seems to indicate that whether or not you're narcissistic has a genetic element and a powerful one. And then it's sort of deterministic and—but then, so how do you wrestle with a problem like that?
4.95: And one of the answers to that is, I don't care what your temperament is. It's going to confer on you a set of advantages, but it's also going to confer on you a set of probable disadvantages. And that'll be the temptations that beckon to you. I studied people who were prone to alcoholism, and they were often people who had multi-generational family histories of alcoholism. And if you gave these people alcohol, their heart rate would go up like 30% after four drinks. And it was because they were responding to alcohol as if it was a cocaine-like, actually an opiate-like psychomotor stimulant.
4.96: And lots of people don't respond to alcohol like that at all. But if you do, you're really going to enjoy alcohol. And you can see that there's a biological component to that. You might think, well, that's radically unfair. And I suppose it is, but it's more complicated than that because your temperament might tilt you towards antisocial behavior, criminality, or narcissism. But it also might tilt you towards, like, sexual licentiousness or neuroticism or depression or anxiety.
4.97: There's going to be a genetic proclivity to some domain of sin for you. But that doesn't mean precisely that it's deterministic. It just means that some things are going to be more tempting for you than others, and you're going to have to wrestle with those things. And other people have to wrestle too, but maybe with different temptations. OK, so that's a good way of thinking about that.
4.98: And you might even be strongly tempted in a particular direction because of your temperament. You're hyper-extroverted and you're hyper-disagreeable, so narcissism is really going to be a temptation. What's the advantage? Well, if you're really extroverted, you have all the advantages of being really extroverted. You're charismatic and dynamic. You like being around other people. You have a lot of energy. You have a lot of positive emotion. And if you're disagreeable, it's bloody difficult for people to take advantage of you. But if you're charismatic and it's difficult to take advantage of you, it's quite easy to take advantage of other people. 4.99 It's like, well, you can't get the advantages without the disadvantages. And then maybe you can be wise enough, if you're bloody likely and careful, lucky and careful, to regulate the temptation and manage to capitalize, let's say, on the advantages. OK, so, back to contemplation. Most people know what sort of hell they would end up in if they allowed themselves to go in that direction. Some people can't control their temper. Some people can't control their drug intake. Some people can't control their despair or their appetite. Who the hell knows where you'd end up if you allowed yourself to fall apart. But you probably have some idea.
4.100: So then, one of the things you can do is, play it out. Imagine what you've done that was stupid in the past, that hurt you. There's probably a pattern of some sort there because people tend to have their pattern of errors. And then you can think, OK, you stop resisting that. You let it take you over completely. What sort of hell are you in, in five years? And maybe you're, I don't know, maybe you're on crank in downtown Portland, bent over. That's you. Is that really what you want?
4.101: And you've got to think it through. Not like some abstraction, but like some deeply embodied fantasy. And you got to think, well, how much do I not want that, and how probable is that, and do I even want to taste it that. Or maybe I just want not to go there at all. And the more real you make it—when you're getting people to expose themselves to things they're afraid of and avoiding, and you get them to do that in their imagination, the more real they make the imagination, which you can measure by measuring their psychophysiological responses.
4.102: Because if you have a frightening fantasy and it's real, you'll sweat more. And that can be measured. The more realistic people make the fantasy, the faster they progress in exposure therapy. And so you can do this with your daydream. It's like, what would you be like if you were as bad as you could be? In the particularized way that you would be the worst you could be? You might think, well, I'd never do that. Well, you should disabuse yourself that thought very, very rapidly. Because that's actually one of the things I learned about totalitarianism.
4.103: It's the people who think they would be least likely to follow the dictates of a totalitarian regime that are in fact the most likely to be exactly those people. It's like, no, it's probably you, buddy. If you can't see it, it just means you're blind. And so this is partly, actually, a grappling with your capability for malevolence, for aiming down. And you can be sure there's things in you that are aiming down. And you might say, well, no, why would I aim down? It's like, ah, you're bitter.
4.104: How would that be? You've been betrayed, you're resentful, you want revenge on other people or maybe yourself, or maybe you want revenge on God for making such a godforsaken reality to begin with. I mean, people have these motivations. If you don't see them, you're not paying attention. And you should pay attention because those motivations, first of all, they get in your way. And second, they might divert you. But even perhaps more importantly, if you get them behind you, pushing you forward, they make you very difficult to stop.
4.105: If you let your fear stop you, well, then you're stopped. But if your fear is propelling you, you're a lot more difficult an agent to interfere with. And so you think— well, one of the reasons, I don't know if this is a good example but it might be. I got myself in trouble about seven years ago for saying some things that people thought I shouldn't say, and the reason I said them was because I was much more afraid of the consequences of losing control of my tongue than I was afraid of whatever the hell the idiot administrators at the university were going to manage to array against me.
4.106: You've got to know what to be afraid of. And one of the things you should be afraid of is your own capacity for self-destructive stupidity. And you can play that out. You think, well, there's a hell I don't think I'm going to visit. But you have to make it real and you have to make it personal, and that's a frightening thing. 5. Faith in Tragedy 5.1 The Christian Passion story nests at the bottom of our culture. And there's a reason for that. It's necessarily the case. And Jung called that story an archetypal tragedy. And this is what he meant by that. It's like the story in the Book of Job. So the Book of Job is a story about a good man. God even admits he's good. And God makes a bet with Satan.
5.2: And Satan comes along and has a chat with God and says, "You think Job is good, but I don't think so. I think he's just fortunate. If you stripped him of everything about his life that would be good, he would become bitter and turn against himself and turn against you." And God says, "Yeah, I don't think so." And Satan says, "Well, why don't you let me have at him and find out?" And God says, "Yes," which is rather a bitter thing for God to do. But there will be definitely times in your life where you feel exactly like that's what's happened to you.
5.3: And so what happens to Job is that almost everything that could possibly be terrible that could happen to a person happens to him. And the story is about how he contends with that. It's a tragedy and an archetypal tragedy. So you might think, what's a tragedy? Well, life is a tragedy. There's tragic aspects to life. And what's a tragedy? Tragedy is when a terrible thing happens to someone. But that can be justice. If you go to a movie and a terrible thing happens to an arch-criminal, you're actually happy about it. You don't think it's a tragedy.
5.4: So it's not merely that terrible things happen. It's that terrible things happen in an unjust way. That's a tragedy. And then you might think, well, what's the ultimate tragedy? And the ultimate tragedy is when the worst possible thing happens to the least possibly deserving person, right? And the reason that that story is at the basis of our culture is because you're going to have to contend with that at some point in your life, because there will be things that will happen to you, despite your innocence, at least in that regard, that make you suffer dreadfully.
5.5: And if it doesn't happen to you, it'll happen to your children, which is a situation that makes it even more poignant and terrible. And so you have to contend with the problem of unjust suffering. And the archetypal story sits at the bottom of our culture because everyone has to contend with that. The Christian Passion is not only the wrestling with tragedy, an unjust tragedy, it's also the harrowing of hell. Part of the mythological dream that surrounds the canonical Judeo-Christian story is that after Christ is crucified, he descends into hell. 5.6 Think, well, what does that mean psychologically, let's say? And what it means is, not only will you have to—every soul has to confront the reality of tragedy and unjust suffering, but that you have to also confront the reality of malevolence. And maybe that's even worse than death. When you look at soldiers who develop post-traumatic stress disorder, most of the time they don't develop that because something terrible has happened to them. They usually develop it because they did something terrible. 5.7 And you find, as a clinician, people can bear an awful lot of suffering even if it's unjust, but if they're betrayed by someone malevolent, especially if it's themselves, they have a hell of a time recovering from that. And so it's very frequently the case that someone who's traumatized isn't traumatized by tragedy. So, for example, if you're four years old and you were sexually molested by your uncle, well, that's not exactly suffering and tragedy, although there may be an element of that, obviously. 5.8 It's betrayal, but it's betrayal of the most perverse sort because it's betrayal by someone who should be taking care of you within the confines of a family, and it's reducing you to an agent of their satisfaction, despite your vulnerability. And then what you have to contend with is not precisely the physical damage that's been done as a consequence of that, although that might be part of it. You have to contend with the fact that now you have to figure out just exactly what the hell motivated that person. And how in the world are you going to do that when you're four? 5.9 Because you can hardly imagine anything darker than that. You can, but that's starting to get pretty far out there on the edge. And one of the things that is done to a four-year-old child who's sexually molested by someone who should be taking care of them is that the problem of the evil in the human heart is laid at their feet when they're four. Now, how in the world are you going to deal with that? What that does is, it just fragments and shatters people.
5.10: Maybe by the time they're 30, maybe they're sophisticated enough to spend a whole year thinking that through and coming up with some formulation about, what would you say, the theological and psychological nature of malevolence itself. And they can put it into context and move on, but it's not an easy matter. Well, one of the things I did with people in my practice who had post-traumatic stress disorder, sometimes people who were betrayed and tortured, sometimes people who'd betrayed themselves, is I'd have them read accounts of great evils.
5.11: So, for example, there's a book called Ordinary Men, a brutal book. And it details—it's really quite a singular book— details out the adventures of this group of policemen who were middle-aged in Nazi Germany. And middle-aged is important because they grew up before the Nazi propaganda. If you grew up under the Nazi propaganda and you became a Nazi, it's like, well, not that that's forgivable, but it's more understandable, because that's all you knew. But if you're, like, 40 when Hitler comes to power, you don't have that as an excuse.
5.12: And so all these policemen in this battalion were middle-aged guys and they're all just ordinary policemen, going about their ordinary policing work in Germany. And then they were shipped as a battalion to Poland when the Germans marched through, and they were basically shanghaied into military service. OK, so now there's a war going on, and the Germans have been told that the reason for the war is the international conspiracy of the evil Jews. And the policemen are told that there's a lot of Jewish people in Poland and that it's necessary for them to keep the peace and keep the homeland safe, to start to act against the Jews.
5.13: And this is a very interesting book because the commander of this battalion was, by all appearances, quite a compassionate and reasonable person. And he told all his policemen at the beginning of the action that if they wanted to leave Poland and go back to Germany and not participate in what was to come, that they could and that there would be no repercussions. And some of them did, and there were no repercussions.
5.14: And by the way, although everyone thinks that, if you didn't abide by the dictatorial dictates of the totalitarian state of Nazi Germany, that you were going to be severely punished. There's not very much evidence for that. People seemed to go along with it voluntarily for the most part, and that was exemplified in this battalion. Well, the first thing these men were called upon to do— now, you might imagine too, you're in that situation now.
5.15: You're out there with all these men you've worked with for a long period of time, and your commander is saying, "Look, we're in a war, and there's going to be some difficult things you have to do. And maybe you don't want to leave all the terrible, difficult things to your comrade here. Maybe you want to shoulder your fair share of the catastrophe." So the people who left, and some of them did, had to do that, despite the fact that in some real sense, they felt they were betrayingtheir fellow officers by leaving them with the dirty work.
5.16: Now, at the beginning, they didn't exactly know what the dirty work was going to be. But I'm telling you this so you can see how the stage might be set for someone's participation. Could easily be that it was the more loyal policemen who stayed. And you generally think that loyalty is an admirable trait. And that's one of the terrible things about participating in great acts of evil, is you can be pulled into them byyour virtues. So that's terrifying. Anyways, they started— I won't get this exactly right, but I get the gist of it.
5.17: They started out, I think they started out by rounding up Jewish men who were of military age and shipping them off to God only knows where, because they didn't really know where they were ending up at that point. But they ended up, step by step, taking naked pregnant women out into the fields and shooting them in the back of the head. And this wasn't a pleasant initiation experience for these men. Most of them developed alcoholism. They were traumatized like mad for doing this.
5.18: But one bloody step at a time, they went along with it until they turned into the absolute worst murderers. And you can be sure that, at some point, some of them started to enjoy it. And then you think, well, what does that have to do with you? And that's a good question. What it has to do with you is that, if you were there, that's probably what you would have done. You think, no, because everyone, you talk to them about this. You talk to people about this, about Nazi Germany, and they always think they're Oskar Schindler. They're the people who would have hid the Jews in the attic.
5.19: It's like, yeah, I don't think so. I don't think so. That was pretty damn rare behavior. If you look at the avidity with which everyone went along with the totalitarian restrictions around Covid, how many people positively enjoyed that? That put paid to any simple notion that we've learned something from what happened 80 years ago. And I would say too, and this is something I learned from Jung, is that, if you are really concerned about the fact that such things happen, and you should be, because they might happen again, and at any moment, you should take whatever steps are necessary to ensure that you wouldn't be a participant.
5.20: And the first thing you have to do is to understand that you probably would be. And since that's the case, there might be some alterations that have to be made to your character that are pretty damn deep. And so, one of the things you do to that is, well, in which handbasket would you ride to go to which particular hell? And what are you doing to increase that probability? And that's a very good thing to meditate on.
5.21: That's also part of the incorporation of the shadow from the Jungian perspective. You can find out some interesting things about yourself, too, because if you're more horrible than you think, which is highly probable, you also might be a more difficult creature to contend with than you might think. Lots of times, people don't really know how to stand up for themselves.
5.22: And this is also part of getting Satan behind you, so to speak, is that if you can get that part of your personality that might make itself manifest in vengefulness and resentment, if you can integrate that and use it as something like what the charismatic power of anger at your fingertips, that makes you very difficult to stop becauseyou'll be facing people who put out a hand to stop you, and often that'll stop people cold. But if you have that demented and bent spirit organized properly in front of you, that's not going to slow you down a bit.
5.23: And that's part of the utility of actually being dangerous. And you're not going to be dangerous till you know you can be. And if you know you can be, well, then you can integrate that. And then you're formidable instead of dangerous, and that's a kind of dangerousness too, but also understanding that can make you treat yourself with a bit more respect. And that respect isn't exactly, let's say, self-esteem. It's more like the respect you might have for a stick of dynamite. Be careful because you don't know what you're capable of.
5.24: So, walk carefully, and don't be thinking that your minor league foolishnesses are, what would you say? Trivial. They're not trivial. What did Dostoevsky say? Solzhenitsyn said, "One man who stops lying can bring down a totalitarian state." So then, if youhappened to inhabit a totalitarian state—maybe that's the job you hate—you might ask yourself, just how much lying are you doing to contribute to that? And if everything around you is turning into a totalitarian state, you might ask yourself the same question. Because maybe if you were a little straighter, things around you wouldn't be quite so crooked.
5.25: And really, I do believe that that is the case and that is the responsibility that rests on every person's shoulders. We wouldn't believe that we are sovereign citizens with intrinsic worth if we weren't charged with that responsibility. And I don't really understand how everyone can be charged with that responsibility, but I do understand that in a totalitarian state, everyone lies about everything all the time. And so then you have to ask yourself, if you refuse to participate, just exactly how much would that shake things up?
5.26: And Solzhenitsyn's conclusion was, well, they'll probably kill you. And maybe that's because you started telling the truth a little late. But I don't know, maybe it's better to risk death than to live in hell. It's something to think about, that's for sure. So this has to do with seriousness, is that one of the things that can make you serious is to really contemplate just how bent and twisted you could become if you allowed yourself to revel in that, let's say.
5.27: I'll give you another example of that. In the story of Cain and Abel, Cain and Abel is a story of sacrifice. It's the story that's placed at the beginning of human history. You could think about it as a story that lays out two broad patterns of adaptation. There's that pattern of Abel, and Abel makes the proper sacrifices. What does that mean? Well, it means something like, he makes the sacrifices that are pleasing to God. OK, so what does that mean? Well, what does it mean to make the proper sacrifices? You know this.
5.28: You know perfectly well when you're giving your all to an enterprise and when you're not. And you know perfectly well that the probability that you'll succeed is proportionate to the amount of commitment you have to the enterprise. Maybe you're like 60% in. You're mucking about and you're trying to get away with things, andyou're a little late to work and you don't do as much of a job as you could and you slough off and, well, you're not going to be that successful and you know that.
5.29: And you probably call yourself out on that, and maybe you've hidden that so much in lies that you've forgotten that you should. And you're all cynical about capitalism so that you can be useless with a good conscience. But you know, and you know this, and you know too that, when you look back at your life and you're pleased with what you've done—genuinely, you'll be pleased because you really put yourself into something. And the consequence of that was that something positive emerged as a consequence. And maybe that's some sort of internal transformation or some sort of material gain or some sort of social gain, like a genuine one.
5.30: And those are the things that put you firmly on your feet. And Abel is a representation of the pattern of proper sacrifice. And Cain, he makes second-rate sacrifices, and that story doesn't really say why. And I think the reason for that is, you have your own reasons for making second-rate sacrifices, and so do you, and the reasons aren't going to be the same. So you don't want to specify that too tightly; you want to leave it loose. It's like, I don't know why you're failing voluntarily. That's in your domain to determine. But the probability that it's the case is very high.
5.31: And why might you do that? The answer has something to do with pride. I mean, when a child attempts to pull the wool over the eyes of his father, he does that because he assumes that his father's too blind and stupid to notice. And that's a form of arrogance. And there's an even deeper arrogance that's associated with it, which is that you're acting out the belief that you can bend and twist the fabric of reality to benefit you unfairly and that there will be no consequences to that.
5.32: That's not a wise decision. Who the hell do you think you are? You really think you can twist what's real and not have it snap back and take you out? That's not a wise conclusion to draw from your experience. Now it's complicated because sometimes you can do that for a short period of time, and it works. And sometimes you can do it for a short-term period of time and it works. And when it snaps back, you can be so blind that you don't draw the connection.
5.33: One of the things you do in therapy is quite painful—and you do this with deep conversations too—if someone's life has taken a vicious turn, you unwind it back to the origin point of that turn, and you generally find that someone made a decision that they knew was an inappropriate decision and that put them on the wrong path. They had their reasons for it. And then they forget, because you don't remember why the hell you did something five years ago. It might take a lot of digging to recreate that state of mind and to remember the decision. But the probability that you knew it was a bad idea when you embarked on it is extremely high.
5.34: That's a painful part of self-realization, because you also have to then come to terms with the fact that, if you took an inappropriate turn five years ago, you've now spent five years erecting the wrong Tower of Babel. That's a good way of thinking about it. All right, so, you sit for 15 minutes and you develop a little vision of just exactly how dismal your bloody life could be if you kept doing all the stupid things you're doing and you did them better. And that's useful. You want to do it to the point where you think, "Yeah, I don't think I'm going to go there."
5.35: And so, then when you're tempted, you see, then in the future, when you're tempted to take a step in that direction, you can conjure up that fantasy and you can think, "Yeah, nah, maybe not, maybe not." And maybe fear isn't enough. And it probably isn't. And it's not the best weapon to use, even though, say, against your proclivity for your worst excesses. And that's why you also need a counter-vision. You need, you need a vision of heaven.
5.36: How would you develop that? Well, it's the same approach about asking and seeking and knocking. It's like, OK, here's the deal. And this is something, you can just do this. It's a useful practice. You can do it for the day or the week or the month, or for five years. Think, "OK, I'm going to give myself the benefit of the doubt, even though maybe I don't deserve it," and that's a hard thing. It's like the presumption of innocence in law. You're going to make the assumption that it would be OK, hypothetically, if things worked out for you.
5.37: Now that's hard, because people bear an existential burden of guilt, and there's always part of us that thinks that we deserve to be punished. And there's often some reality to that, but flawed as you are, you might still be worthy. This is the conclusion Job comes to, by the way, when he's tormented. There's two things—he doesn't lose the thread. Two threads.
5.38: One, he maintains faith in his own value despite the fact that he's suffering dreadfully. And his friends come along and say, "You're probably suffering because you're bad, because you're unworthy, because you're sinful, because you've done stupid things." And Job says, "Well, I probably have done stupid things like people do, but that doesn't mean that my suffering invalidates my own merit." And that's a very tricky thing to get right. Because if you're down on the ground and things are rough in your life at the moment, it's going to be a temptation to take yourself out.
5.39: Well, and I mean, sometimes literally, people will commit suicide to assume that you're such a dismal creature that it would be better if you didn't exist and maybe that you never had. And so you can understand how you might get to that point. And Job refuses to walk down that road, even though everything he ends up with, like this terrible disfiguring skin disease, and he loses everything he spent his whole life gaining. And his wife is so desperate that she tells him to "shake his fist at God and die," which is pretty rough advice.
5.40: And then his friends come along and tell him how horrible he is and why he deserves everything that's happened to him. So it's pretty damn rough. But one of the things that he insists upon is that, despite the tragedy of his life, he has intrinsic merit. And the story is more powerful, too, because we have God's testimony at the beginning of the story that Job is, in fact, a good man. He's not just making this up. He's not justifying himself falsely.
